answer: Two analysts can view the same scatter plot of community health worker program intensity against preventable hospitalizations and reach opposite policy recommendations because correlation alone does not identify a causal effect. The disagreement turns on identification: whether the variation in program intensity reflects the program's impact or selection, since county capacity affects both program adoption and health outcomes. Without an exogenous source of variation, such as randomized funding or a budget cutoff affecting otherwise-similar counties, the causal effect of the program cannot be separated from the counties that would have done better regardless.

faqs.q: How can the same data support opposite policy conclusions?
faqs.a: When an effect is not identified, the same correlation is consistent with the program working or with high-capacity counties simply adopting it and performing better anyway. Each analyst's recommendation reflects a different untested assumption about which story is true.

faqs.q: What does identification mean in causal inference?
faqs.a: Identification is having a source of variation in treatment that lets you distinguish the treatment's effect from selection. Here it would require variation in CHW funding driven by something other than county capacity or political will.

faqs.q: What kind of variation would identify the CHW program effect?
faqs.a: Variation unrelated to county capacity, such as a policy that randomly assigned CHW funding or a budget cutoff that affected otherwise-similar counties differently, would separate the program effect from selection.
